children: By Dominic Chopping and Mauro Orru

Alphabet's Google said it would spend more than $15 billion to develop artificial-intelligence infrastructure in Finland, the latest big-ticket commitment from a U.S. tech giant to bolster its AI capacity overseas.

The company said the investment of at least 13 billion euros, equivalent to $15.11 billion, would fund data centers and other infrastructure, including clean energy projects, between 2027 and 2028 across four locations.

The commitment, which Google said was its largest single investment in Europe, underscores the company's efforts to expand operations overseas in a bid to capitalize on growing demand for AI services.

Tech giants have pledged billions of dollars to beef up data centers, cloud services and AI infrastructure in Europe since OpenAI's release of ChatGPT to the public in late 2022 ushered in a spending frenzy.

Earlier this year, Amazon.com said it would invest 33.7 billion euros through 2035 to bolster its cloud and data-center infrastructure in Spain, while Microsoft said in September last year that it would pour $30 billion into AI infrastructure and existing operations in the U.K. through 2028.

Google already has a data center in Hamina on Finland's south coast-the site of a former paper mill that it bought in 2009 and converted. The financing outlined Wednesday includes fresh investments there and at other sites to develop digital infrastructure to power services like Gemini, Search, Maps and YouTube.
As part of its digital infrastructure build-out in the country, Google also said it was allocating funds to new energy capacity, grid enhancements and energy affordability initiatives.

Google's investment pledge is a win for Finnish President Alexander Stubb, a European leader who has forged an unexpected bond with President Trump. During the initial construction phase, the initiative is expected to contribute billions of dollars to Finland's economy and support more than 37,000 jobs. Once operational, Google said the facilities are projected to support 7,000 jobs.

The company has also signed power-purchase agreements with domestic onshore wind-power providers and contracted a new battery system to connect to Finland's grid. That is aimed at helping with grid balancing and stabilizing electricity prices.

Shares of Fortum jumped more than 8% on Wednesday after the Nordic energy group said it had signed a 22-year power-purchase agreement with Google that would enable it to extend the life of its Loviisa nuclear power plant.
Under the agreement, Google will buy 50% of the plant's capacity from 2030 through 2049.
